title: The next doubling
hook: World population doubled faster and faster. Did the latest doubling keep up the pace?

knows: world population grew fast and passed 8 billion
doesNotKnow: that the last doubling (4 to 8 billion) took no less time than the one before
that the yearly growth rate peaked in 1963

misconception: World population keeps doubling faster and faster.
objective: The learner can say that world population's doublings took 122, 48 and 47 years, so the last was no faster than the one before, and that growth per year peaked in 1963 (2.25%) and has fallen since (0.87% in 2023).

claims.source: history-data.mjs: gmpop, gapminder-pop-global.csv, column pop (Gapminder Fast Track; estimates before 1950). The values for 1800-2023 are copied into Demo.tsx unchanged (v2: the 2024 value is no longer in the array); the stage draws to 2023 only. history-cycle2-check.mjs section 15.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Re-derived in my own node script from the pinned file (history-data.mjs pins all hold; sha256 re-checked) and compared with the copied array in Demo.tsx (identical). POP in Demo.tsx = the file's pop column 1800-2024 (225 values, identical); stage draws to 2023. | v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-15): source field only: POP now ends at 2023 (2024 dropped, FC39/FC41 c3). claims.text: World population first reached 1 billion in 1805, 2 billion in 1927, 4 billion in 1975 and 8 billion in 2022: the doublings took 122 years, then 48, then 47.
claims.source: First year with pop >= 1e9, 2e9, 4e9, 8e9 in the column. Computed in Demo.tsx; history-cycle2-check.mjs section 15 '15 doubling years'.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): First year >= threshold: 1 bn 1805 (1,002,667,483), 2 bn 1927, 4 bn 1975, 8 bn 2022 (8,021,407,192). 122, 48, 47. Same in Demo.tsx firstAt().

claims.text: Growth per year peaked at 2.25% in 1963 (1963 to 1964) and was 0.88% from 2022 to 2023.
claims.source: Growth labelled by its start year y = 100 x (pop[y+1] / pop[y] - 1), using values up to 2023 only; peak over 1900-2022: 1963, 100 x (P1964/P1963 - 1) = 2.245, shown 2.25. Last rate 100 x (P2023/P2022 - 1) = 100 x (8,091,734,930 / 8,021,407,192 - 1) = 0.877, shown 0.88. Re-derived in node from the pinned file 2026-10-15. The stage labels it '2022 to 2023'. Note: history-cycle2-check.mjs section 15 still computes g23 = gr(2023), which needs the 2024 value; its amend to the 2022 to 2023 rate is cm-history's (W-869).
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): The peak holds (forward rate 100 x (P[y+1]/P[y] - 1) peaks at 2.245% in 1963; backward rate gives the same 2.245% labelled 1964). The 2023 figure does not hold as a record. 0.87% is pop(2024)/pop(2023) - 1, and the file's pop concept is v8 dated 'July 29, 2024' (ddf--concepts.csv, opened). A mid-2024 value published in July 2024 cannot be a counted record. It is a projection or a nowcast. The lesson's own limit sentence says the chart stops at the present and 'any later number is a projection, not a record', so the stage contradicts its own limit. I could not open Gapminder's pop documentation (gapm.io/dpop is unreachable) to see where its estimates end. Fix (history-builder): use only values up to 2023. Either (a) a backward rate throughout, 100 x (P[y]/P[y-1] - 1), giving peak 2.25% in 1964 and 0.88% in 2023, or (b) keep the forward rate and label the last value '2022 to 2023: 0.88%'. Then drop 2024 from POP. Either way the reveal says 0.88%, not 0.87%. Also bring the check script (history-cycle2-check.mjs section 15) into line. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): DISPUTED. STILL DISPUTED (Demo.tsx unchanged since pass 39: POP still runs to 2024 and the 2023 rate is pop(2024)/pop(2023) - 1). New supporting evidence, opened: OWID 'What are the sources for Our World in Data's population estimates?' (ourworldindata.org/population-sources): the UN World Population Prospects give 'Annual historical estimates running from 1950 to the year before the most recent dataset publication; Annual projections running from the year of the most recent dataset publication'. Gapminder pop v8 is dated 29 July 2024 (ddf--concepts.csv), so its 2024 value is at best a same-year projection, not a record, which the lesson's own limit sentence (c5) rules out. Fix unchanged (history-builder): backward rate 100 x (P[y]/P[y-1] - 1), giving 2.25% in 1964 and 0.88% in 2023, or keep the forward rate and label the last value '2022 to 2023: 0.88%'; drop 2024 from POP; align history-cycle2-check.mjs section 15. | v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-15): FC39/FC41 c3 fix (option b) and cm-history ruling: forward rate kept, last value is 2022 to 2023, 0.88%; 2024 dropped from POP; was '0.87% in 2023'. Reset to unverified for a fact-checker who is not the builder. | FC pass 43 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Stage: 'peak 2.25% in 1963; 0.88%, 2022 to 2023', chart labels 'peak 1963: 2.25%' and '2022 to 2023: 0.88%'; reveal 'peaked at 2.25% in 1963 and was 0.88% from 2022 to 2023'. Own node script on the pinned gapminder-pop-global.csv (sha256 84e8705b... matches the pin): 100 x (3,264,487,339 / 3,192,807,828 - 1) = 2.24503 -> 2.25, the maximum over start years 1900-2022; 100 x (8,091,734,930 / 8,021,407,192 - 1) = 0.8768 -> 0.88. Demo.tsx POP = the file's 224 values 1800-2023, 0 mismatches; no 2024 value. Gapminder concept 'pop' is v8, 29 July 2024 (ddf--concepts.csv, opened), i.e. after UN WPP 2024, so 2023 is the last estimate year. Advisory, not blocking: the rate is not monotonic after 1963 (2021 to 2022 was 0.84%, so the last rate is slightly up), and history-cycle2-check.mjs still computes gr(2023) (W-869).

claims.text: The last doubling was about as fast as the one before; a doubling that takes as long as the last one, at a falling yearly rate, means growth is slowing, not racing.
claims.source: Doubling time is set by the yearly rate (math:exponential-growth); 47 vs 48 years (c2), within the one-year resolution of 'first year at or above', and the rate falls after the 1963 peak (c3).
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Follows from c2, c3: 47 vs 48 years, and the rate falls after the 1960s peak. Wording note, not blocking: the reveal says 'the last was no faster than the one before'. Read literally, 47 < 48 is one year faster, though that is within the one-year resolution of 'first year above'. Suggest 'about as fast as the one before'. | v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-15): FC39 c4 wording note: reveal 'no faster than the one before' became 'about as fast as the one before', and that clause is now in this claim's text. Reset to unverified for a fact-checker who is not the builder. | FC pass 43 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Reveal: 'the last was about as fast as the one before. ... A doubling that takes as long as the last one, at a falling yearly rate, means growth is slowing, not racing.' Spans 48 and 47 years at first-year resolution; by linear interpolation of the crossings they are 47.5 and 47.6, so 'about as fast' is right and 'faster' would not be. Average rate over each doubling 1.48% (1927-1975) and 1.45% (1975-2022); yearly rate 1.81% in 1975, 0.88% in 2022 to 2023. Growth slowing, not accelerating, holds.

claims.text: Where it stops: early totals are the least certain, and the chart stops at the present; any later number is a projection, not a record.
claims.source: Brief 15 limit sentence. 'Early totals are the least certain': OWID 'The Spanish flu' endnote ('precise annual counts of the world population are not available for the past ... the annual estimates are interpolations') and OWID 'What are the sources for Our World in Data's population estimates?' (ourworldindata.org/population-sources: decadal HYDE estimates 1800-1950, annual UN WPP estimates from 1950), both opened by FC41. 'The chart stops at the present; any later number is a projection': true by construction (POP ends at 2023).
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Second half verified by definition (the stage stops at 2023; values after the present are projections). First clause 'early totals are the least certain' has no opened source. The pin description's 'estimates before 1950' is the pin author's note; it is not in ddf--concepts.csv or the open-numbers READMEs I opened. Fix (builder, as the source field offers): cut the clause, giving 'Where it stops: the chart stops at the present; any later number is a projection, not a record.' | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Learner text (Demo.tsx line 213): 'Where it stops: early totals are the least certain, and the chart stops at the present; any later number is a projection, not a record.' The first clause, held in pass 39, is now supported by opened OWID pages. 'The Spanish flu' article (ourworldindata.org/spanish-flu-largest-influenza-pandemic-in-history), endnote: 'precise annual counts of the world population are not available for the past. Instead historians try to reconstruct the population figures for 5-year or 10-year intervals and the annual estimates are interpolations between these estimates.' The 'population sources' page says HYDE estimates 'are only available once per decade for the period 1800-1950' and that Gapminder's 1800-1949 series is built on Maddison and Clio Infra reconstructions, while UN WPP gives annual estimates from 1950. The second clause is true by definition (the stage stops at 2023). Note: c3's dispute is separate. It is the 2024 value inside the 2023 growth rate, not this sentence. | v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-15): source field only: cites the pages FC41 opened. The task asked to cut the first clause (the FC39 fix), but FC41 verified the sentence as it stands, so the learner text is unchanged and the status kept.

claims.text: World population doubled faster and faster (hook): 1 to 2 billion took 122 years, 2 to 4 billion took 48.
claims.source: c2: 1927 - 1805 = 122; 1975 - 1927 = 48 (history-cycle2-check.mjs section 15). The hook states only the first two doublings; the third is the question.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Hook: 1927-1805 = 122, 1975-1927 = 48 (c2). 'Doubled faster and faster' is true of those two spans.

recall.question: A town grows from 10,000 to 20,000 in 30 years, then to 40,000 in the next 30. Is its growth speeding up?
options: No: the same doubling time is the same rate
recall.why: Adding more people each period is what steady percentage growth looks like; only a shorter doubling time would mean speeding up.
